author: Wini Omer
title: It’s not the refugees, it’s the austerity measures!
content:
A Sudanese journalist, with whom I worked for two years at the same newspaper, told me when I contacted him to check on his situation after the last wave of attacks against refugees in Libya: “We are trapped in our homes. We can’t leave. I didn’t send my kids to school since the beginning of this wave of violence. The situation is difficult beyond imagination.”

The Sudanese who left Sudan seeking refuge in Libya, amid very violent clashes that started in April 2023 and continue to this moment, are facing violence, danger, and hatred in what was supposed to be a safe refuge. But this reality is not exclusive to Sudanese refugees, and the violence is indifferent to other nationalities who are fleeing conflicts, war, and instability at home: Ethiopians, Eritreans, and refugees from the Central African Republic.

In Libya, African refugees faced waves of violence, the latest in June this year. Despite competing for power, Libya’s rival authorities in the east and west have united in stoking anti-migrant rhetoric and launching a violent campaign of mass detention and expulsions against migrants and refugees, as a recent 

Human Rights Watch report

 has indicated.

In Egypt, a 

crackdown campaign

 led by security forces, accompanied by social media hate speech against Sudanese and Syrian refugees, intensified on the ground, blaming them for the rise in living costs, mainly rents, groceries, and basic life needs. As a result of systematic brutality, between January and June 2026, 

12 Sudanese passed away in Egyptian detention centers

 and police cells, including a child of 17. Refugees processed for deportation are forced to sign voluntary return declarations.

Sudan hosts one of the largest refugee and asylum-seeker populations in Africa, mainly South Sudanese, Ethiopians, and Eritreans, who currently face detention and 

forced deportation

 from the capital, Khartoum, to refugee camps close to the borders with their countries of origin, after the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) regained control of the capital. This step was taken following a growing political rhetoric that profiled them as criminals and blamed them for the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) controlling Khartoum. Accordingly, they were deported to refugee camps in White Nile State, Al-Gadarif State, and Kassala State, camps that lack all basic human needs and restrict freedom of movement and the right to work. Many South Sudanese mothers were deported while their children were not allowed to accompany them, leaving them in limbo.

Such rhetoric, mainly produced and shared by pro-SAF individuals and platforms, provides the military establishment with a popular cover to reproduce its symbolic authority. It is also used by some actors within the army as a tool to bolster its legitimacy against the Rapid Support Forces, portraying it as the guardian of national sovereignty and the representative of the “authentic Sudanese” against the “foreign threat.” This reflects a deeper attempt to regain control over the state and society at a moment of total collapse of political and legal frameworks.

For many of these refugees, especially the Eritreans, returning is not an option, considering the human rights situation in Eritrea. But according to media reports, both Eritrea and Sudan are 

complicit in the repatriation of civilians from Sudan

 back to Eritrea.

Whether it is the systematic violence against Sudanese refugees on the continent, or the deliberate violence against African refugees in Sudan, these incidents reflect one broader reality in which violence is used and reproduced either by state actors or by the citizens of the host countries to whom the refugees sought safety within the African continent. This reality raises a critical question about how to understand such incidents, the politics behind them, and why we are seeing them now.

Shifting the blame

Have the refugees led to the economic crises in Egypt, Libya, or Tunisia? Or are these crises a direct result of the state’s social and economic policies?

In Egypt, the last ten years have witnessed a high level of dependence on debt; Egypt has become one of the IMF’s largest borrowers, while social expenditure, including social protection, health, and education, has shrunk, accompanied by political oppression. Those debts have been invested in projects lacking a developmental dimension, such as 

the new administrative capital

 project, which is expected to cost up to $300 billion by the time it’s finalized. The new capital is home to Africa’s tallest 

tower

, the world’s longest 

monorail

, and a new presidential palace commissioned by President Sisi. This tells the story of the political crisis through spatial isolation: Government ministries and parliament have been moved kilometers away from the historic urban spaces where demonstrations and revolutions were shaped. It is also heavily securitized through surveillance and the military, shifting budgets away from serving the people toward strict monitoring. State resources and national debt constrain the broader economy and exacerbate poverty and social inequalities.

Higher external debt interest payments, in addition to the 

cost of arms imports

, which increased by 215 percent in 2013–2017 compared to 2008–2012, led to an economic crisis. Debt has also been a tool for maintaining a grip on citizens, while the military’s economic empire has expanded. It’s also worth noting that 1,365 conditions were imposed by the IMF and World Bank on MENA nations over the last 15 years, enforcing austerity, privatization, and deregulation. Conditionality has shaped the social and economic realities in many countries across the globe.

The state has slowly 

moved away from the bread subsidy system

 over the past ten years of International Monetary Fund–guided policy adjustments. This economic crisis has also contributed to the 

rise in immigration rates

 among Egyptians to Gulf countries and beyond.

This pattern aligns with Samir Amin’s critique: Peripheral states are integrated into global capitalism in ways that prioritize capital accumulation and elite prestige over popular welfare.

In Libya, the political and economic crises have intersected, creating a hostile environment for refugees. The cash-flow crisis stemming from multiple changes to national currency notes, high unemployment rates, deterioration of social services, electricity instability, and a health-care system that is not adequately accessible to the population have compounded the situation. All of these crises are a direct result of years of conflict and political instability.

It’s also a direct consequence of imperialist intervention in Libya. NATO and US military operations in Libya, the sanctions, and the border-engineering policies financed by the EU have all resulted in building a racist architecture. Resources received from the EU were used to establish influential militias, including the Libyan Coast Guard, now running smuggling and human trafficking economies that are 

sanctioned by the UN

, even as they continue to receive EU 

funding and training

.

Similarly, Tunisia has been 

trapped in debt

. The social justice demands that ignited the 2010 revolution were not addressed; instead, an oppressive system is maintaining itself.

Such crises have led to high unemployment rates and rising poverty, fueling both the desire among young people to emigrate and scapegoating narratives against refugees promoted by those who stayed.

The South African case provides a clear example of this shift in blame. In a country with an unemployment rate of over 43.7 percent, protests against migrants have intensified in recent months, primarily led by the 

March and March

 movement, blaming African migrants for unemployment, poverty, crime, and lack of public services like education and health care. They called on the government to deal with the influx of migrants and protect opportunities. While it’s understandable that material despair and fear drive these protests, the root causes of this compounded crisis cannot be ignored. That includes the legacy of apartheid and the lack of economic justice post-independence. The white population, which constitutes 8 percent of the whole South African population, controls around 80 percent of the land, leaving the majority of the population, Black and coloured, with no ownership of land or means of production. With little being done to implement the social justice agenda in the post-apartheid state, wealth has remained concentrated among the same elite class, while the majority remain impoverished.

Adopting social and economic policies that impoverish people and limit their access to social services and basic needs is a key feature of the approaches in Egypt, Tunisia, Libya, and South Africa, among many other countries. This strategy is universal and aims to collectively punish populations to protect the systems that exploit them.

Refugees are being blamed for the difficult material conditions of citizens in crisis-affected countries, even though these conditions have their own political and historical structural causes and are closely linked to the political economies of states that are often highly dependent on the profiteering monetary and financial policies of international financial institutions.

Politics of hate and fear

But how are the political and economic crises entangled with hatred or fear of refugees?

Sara Ahmed’s 

The Cultural Politics of Emotion

 sheds light on how an anti-refugee sentiment is built, encouraged, and used to justify violence against them, and how building a national identity comes at the cost of the safety of refugees.

Fear is employed as a tool of political economy and as a technique of governance. In the Egyptian case, fear of refugees burdening the state’s budget is used to justify current social and economic crises and to trap people into relying on the political elite, represented by those in government, to resolve the refugee dilemma. Sudanese, Palestinian, and Syrian refugees have been labeled as such, and Sudanese refugees have lost their lives due to the security policies and interventions that forcibly deport them. A recent anti-refugee narrative relates to fear of what is called the “Afrocentrism discourse,” as many social media accounts share concerns over deliberate efforts by Black refugees to change the culture and demography of Egypt.

Fear of demographic change is echoed more loudly in official political speeches in Tunisia. President Kais Saied 

reflected on

 this specific issue during an official speech, while the crackdown on human rights activists continues, and voices that criticized the economic situation in Tunisia are silenced. Additionally, a 

Tunisian MP used racist language to deny reports

 on female refugees being sexually assaulted in Tunisia.

In Libya as well, such discourse spreads on social media, provoked by politicians seeking to build constituencies based on this fear.

On the other hand, Egyptian media portray refugees as the 

main cause of the crisis

 and as a burden on the social infrastructure, such as health and housing. On social media, these campaigns were led by 

pro-regime influencers

, as some fact-checking platforms have indicated.

Syrian refugees and immigrants in Egypt also suffer from this manufactured fear through campaigns, including calls to boycott their businesses, accusing them of hijacking market opportunities.

Similarly, in Sudan, long before April’s war, refugees have faced accusations of immorality and been labeled as a danger to the Sudanese community’s values and social cohesion. Burdening refugees with the responsibility of security and treating them as a threat to national security are also narratives used, especially by the Sudanese army, to justify the forcible deportation of refugees to camps.

Such narratives act as a political strategy: Fear is engineered to elicit collective emotions and utilized in political discourse to mask the flaws of political regimes.

Fanon’s critique of postcolonial elites is relevant in the contexts above; he argued that elites turn the people against imaginary enemies. In this case, refugees are those imaginary enemies.

The failures of neoliberal policy

The shared economic model of these states centers on austerity and privatization policies that aim to limit state spending on social infrastructure and services, while using securitization and violence to suppress any attempts to protest against these policies. This explains why Egyptian arms deals increase as the economy deteriorates.

Refugees are usually forcibly displaced by economic collapse, structural adjustment, climate harm, and governance failure. They are then governed through restrictive asylum regimes, border controls, and humanitarian management. So neoliberal policies help produce displacement and then shape how displaced people are subsequently controlled.

In other cases, we have seen the externalization of borders as a strategy that has allowed states to avoid direct responsibility for violating refugees’ rights. The EU is infamous for leading such strategies. Such policies often come with loans and financial support to the targeted origin and transit countries.

Tunisia has also received such support, leading to a refugee crisis, as thousands are 

trapped in Tunisia

, most of them from sub-Saharan Africa, in a very dire situation, while some have been dumped into the Algerian desert to face their fate.

Previously, the Rapid Support Forces received EU support to control borders in eastern and western Sudan. The Khartoum Process, which evolved into a regional agreement, brokered this deal and provided funding for border externalization.

The European Union Horn of Africa Migration Route Initiative (the 

Khartoum Process

) is a political cooperation platform launched on November 28, 2014, in Rome. It connects countries along the migration route from the Horn of Africa to Europe.

Libya’s decision to ban the entry of citizens from four African nationalities — Sudan, Eritrea, Ethiopia, and Somalia — is also understood as part of these broader policies. Libya was actually among the first countries to receive EU funds to control the influx of refugees at its borders. Meanwhile, 

Greece is recruiting mercenaries

 to push back refugees. Alongside these trends, 

the EU Parliament’s recent law

 reveals a similar stance, with members shouting “send them back” as a law to return refugees was adopted.

From Europe, to Africa, to Southeast Asia, refugees are facing violence, exclusion, and impoverishment. These are the direct social damages of neoliberal policies, generating economic exploitation and social exclusion, and stripping refugees of their dignity and their lives, as is happening right now in Egypt, in Libya, and on the coasts of the Mediterranean Sea.

The Sudanese refugee crisis was ignited by the ongoing war in Sudan; it’s rooted in a long history of conflicts that have driven thousands to leave their homes in search of refuge and dignity. The crises in Sudan that have led to conflict can’t be understood without tracing the histories of austerity, uneven development, and state violence.

Sudanese refugees deserve safety and protection, just like refugees on the African continent and beyond.

Political rhetoric centered on anti-Blackness and blame-shifting must be dismantled to center critiques on the role of capitalism and neoliberal policies. Systems that exploit refugees as cheap labor and as bodies that should produce surplus value must be exposed.

Instead of considering refugees as the problem, we should view them and their vulnerabilities as manifestations of social and economic crises manufactured by neoliberalism, and as direct products of political decisions that fail to center care, justice, and economic sovereignty. The nation-state survives by dividing people, provoking hatred and fear, and stoking competition. We, the oppressed people, must resist.

author: Elyas Mabchour
title: Morocco’s long game
content:
“A bad system will beat a good person every time.” The words of Dr. Deming, a pioneer of systems thinking, perfectly encapsulate the problems faced by Moroccan football throughout the 2000s. 

At the turn of the century, on paper, it seemed like Moroccan football was in a pretty good place. In 1998, it was ranked 13th globally by FIFA. The team’s performance at the 1986 World Cup, when Morocco became the first African and Arab country to advance to the knockout rounds, was monumental.

Despite these early successes, Morocco would subsequently not qualify for a World Cup for the next 20 years. By 2014, Moroccan football would hit rock bottom, with FIFA ranking it 81st in the world — a precipitous decline. 

But as many of us know, by 2022 Morocco had risen to the top of international football. The team defeated major World Cup players, such as Portugal and Spain, becoming the first African and Arab country to advance to the semifinals. 

To me, the answer to Morocco’s football transformation comes down to one thing: systems (and I think Dr. Deming would be happy with that conclusion).

The reason behind Morocco’s 2000s decline was simple: Morocco relied on a series of golden generations that emerged around the end of the 20th century. After 

Morocco entered a World Bank Structural Adjustment Program to address the country’s debts in 1983

, key sources of state funding for local sport were cut off as the country recovered economically. Without an effective system for replacing players as they retired, the sport would naturally start to decline. 

Morocco’s rise after that initial decline was more complex. As I began exploring this story, I came across a turning point: the 2008 Skhirat Conference. Recognizing football’s unique position to drive national pride and social cohesion across a young demographic, the King took the rare step of intervening directly, calling for reforms in football governance and investment at all levels in what is now known as the 

Royal Letter 2008

. The letter attributed the sport’s decline to corruption and mismanagement, as well as the decentralized nature of sports across the country. The King argued that Moroccan football’s problem was not talent, but the absence of a national system to develop it. 

The first and most consequential change was the appointment of Fouzi Lekjaa as president of the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FRMF) in 2014. Despite Lekjaa’s middle-class origins, the Berkane native very quickly took to politics, developing his reputation as a shrewd and clever leader. Lekjaa spent years as Director of the Budget at the Ministry of Economy and Finance, while on the pitch, he served as president of RS Berkane, bringing crucial fiscal governance to state sports policy and guiding his club to a historic 2012 Botola Pro promotion. As FRMF president, Lekjaa stated that going forward, 

Moroccan football would rely on a three-pronged approach: facilities, talent, and well-trained staff.

 

An early example of this approach was the opening of the Mohammed VI Football Academy in Salé in 2009 as a 140 million dirham ($14.4 million USD) project aimed at developing homegrown talent. In the following years, alumni such as Azzedine Ounahi and Youssef En-Nesyri would go on to represent Morocco at the 2022 World Cup, while many others joined the U17 and U20 teams.

The federation pushed clubs to strengthen their youth-development structures, creating more organized pathways to identify and train young players, while academy staff scouted talent nationwide. The academy’s first director, Nasser Larguet, would travel the country with his team, observing 15,000 young players and ultimately selecting 37 to come and train at the academy. This pipeline showed Morocco could grow talent at home, rather than relying solely on the diaspora. 

Yet, the diaspora remains a major source of talent for Moroccan football. The 2026 World Cup prompted headlines that 

Morocco was the first team in World Cup history to feature a lineup of players who were all born outside of the country they represented

. But this headline reflects a longer-term strategy: with around 15% of all Moroccans living abroad, primarily in Europe, Morocco spent years building an extensive diaspora scouting and recruitment network. 

The system would identify eligible talent at a young age, with coordinator Rabie Takassa saying that their network identifies talent as early as eight years old

. By leveraging both home-grown and diaspora talent, Morocco built two talent pipelines that fed into national teams, broadening the pool of players available to the federation.

This system would go on to work. Yassine Bounou was ranked 4th on the list of the 2026 tournament’s top-performing goalkeepers, according to the 

FIFA Power Rankings

. He spent years playing with Wydad AC in Casablanca before transitioning to European football. Through the other pipeline, Brahim Diaz would develop his skills at Málaga CF and then Manchester City’s academy, representing Spain multiple times at the youth level. Both opted to play for the Moroccan national team at the senior level. 

Some may argue that Morocco is simply witnessing another “random” golden generation. Yet the U20 team’s 2025 World Cup victory and the senior team’s 2026 quarterfinal run suggest a more systematic change. Morocco proved it could consistently play at the level of football’s best, matching Brazil and defeating the Netherlands. The Kingdom exited the tournament ranked 6th globally by FIFA, a striking contrast with its 81st-place ranking in 2014.

The challenges facing African football often extend beyond a lack of talent to the systems needed to develop players and bring them to the global stage, especially at a senior level. 

Nigeria, for example, holds the record for the most U-17 World Cup wins, but this hasn’t translated to comparable success at the senior level

. The gap highlights a broader challenge facing African football federations: developing talent at the youth level is only a part of the task. Moroccan football offers a case study for the rest of the continent, an example of how systems can drastically improve a country’s football fortunes. 

Morocco would begin its journey to becoming a football powerhouse when it stopped waiting for golden generations to spontaneously emerge and began building the systems needed to constantly find and develop the talent required to compete at the highest level.

author: Rachel Dubale
title: Eyes open in Addis
content:
If I squeeze my eyes shut and cover them with my hands, perhaps all of this will disappear. My father used to tell me something similar when, at an age perhaps already too old for it, I would whisper to him: “I’m afraid of the dark.”

“

Richo

,” he would say, “why in the world would you be scared of the dark? The dark is something we can make and unmake. See?” He would then cover my eyes with his big, calloused hands. “I made the dark for you.” And so I would fall asleep, covering my eyes with my hands and making my own dark.

So many years have passed since then — years in which I have learned not only how to make my own dark, but how to fill my eyes with the brightest colors: the green of my fields, the yellow suns of the Antilles, and the red of those tomato sauces shared over plates of pasta with the people I love.

With time I have also learned, and wanted 

more

 and 

more

 and 

more

, to see and live those same colors lined up in a row: green-yellow-red. And again: green-yellow-red, the flag of my country of origin, Ethiopia. Sometimes for a few months at a time, during summers spent in the capital; sometimes buried in tedious readings, retracing its legendary history; other times — for longer, for months — trying to learn its script, so curved, as I did when I lived in Addis Ababa from September 2022 into 2023.

That time, in 2022, when I spent several months in the capital, is perhaps one of the times I most distinctly remember feeling like a child again: trying to memorize the 

fidel

, the Ethiopic script, from the blackboard, slowly reading one letter after another, and then hoping that somehow a sentence that made sense in Amharic would come out of my mouth.

Perhaps it was also one of those times when, unconsciously becoming a little like a child again — learning how to read and write in a new language, discovering everything from scratch — I decided to do what my father had told me years before and cover my eyes with my hands.

By the time I arrived in Addis Ababa, the war in Tigray — mainly, but not solely, pitting Tigrayan forces led by the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) against the Ethiopian federal government — had been going on for almost two years. Just two months later, in November, the two sides signed the so-called 

Pretoria Agreement

, committing to a permanent cessation of hostilities. And yet, even in the capital, at least to me, the war and the tensions it had brought to the surface continued to come in fragments.

I remember, in order:

When the war came knocking at the edges of the city. That January of 2023 I was walking through the streets of Asko, right at the edge of the capital, wearing a traditional Wollo dress from the Amhara region.

All dressed up with my cousins, we hummed songs to celebrate Timket, the Ethiopian Orthodox festival marking the baptism of Jesus in the River Jordan, and were laughing our heads off about who had been hit by the most lemons — during Timket, young men traditionally toss lemons or limes toward girls they are interested in, as a sort of courtship — when some police officers on the street told us to keep it down. “And then,” they added, “you should be ashamed of wearing those clothes. We are celebrating Timket, not one particular ethnic group.” Ouch.

It took me, in fact, a little while — and an explanation from my cousins — to understand what I had initially taken as an insult to my sense of style. The traditional Amhara dress, it turned out, was not read simply as a dress but almost as a political statement in support of Amhara identity amid tensions around ethnicity — who was who, who was supposedly better than whom — that had been growing for years and that the war in Tigray had only exacerbated.

Funnily enough, this happened just as Amhara forces, which had fought alongside Ethiopian federal troops during the war, were reportedly 

beginning to withdraw

 from parts of Tigray, seemingly in line with the provisions of the Pretoria Agreement. Yet on the streets of Addis, some of the tensions left by the war were proving harder to leave behind.

Something similar happened, for similar reasons, when I was denied access to my own home. Every March, Addis Ababa dresses itself in green-yellow-red to commemorate the majestic victory at the Battle of Adwa in 1896, when Ethiopian troops, led by Emperor Menelik II and Empress Taytu Betul, defeated the invading Italian army. Yet that year, even a victory remembered as pan-Ethiopian seemed to 

fracture

 along ethnic lines. Menelik, celebrated by many as a symbol of Ethiopian independence, was also remembered by others for the violence and dispossession that accompanied his empire’s expansion into territories inhabited by different ethnic communities in what is now Ethiopia.

By then, displaying images of Emperor Menelik and Empress Taytu, or even the plain Ethiopian flag without its central emblem, had become politically contentious, as these symbols were increasingly associated with competing visions of Ethiopian identity. Printing presses and shops selling them were reportedly forced to shut down.

And by Adwa Bridge, where I lived, the roads had been blocked amid the tensions around the celebrations, and so, for hours and hours, my flatmate and I tried to make our way home but were not allowed through, left outside waiting until it was dark and then darker.

And finally, the countless times when, beyond the celebrations, the war found its way into people’s mouths, as they told me how they tried, and tried again, to reach their loved ones in the North, where phone lines had been cut off for much of the war.

Yet, as unreal as all of this felt to me, I realize now how little it changed in my everyday life. As with the thousand other incredible injustices of the world, I carried on with my life, while kilometers away from me, within the very same borders, thousands of people were being hit, dispossessed, and killed (among other things).

Four years have passed since then and now history repeats itself: I find myself, again, in Addis Ababa. Across the country, fighting has erupted again between federal and Tigrayan forces, with former enemies joining forces against the government under a new coalition calling itself the 

Alliance for Survival

. But this time I am better trained: I can now read with ease all the news I have to compile for work in Amharic: 

Turmoil in Tigray

; 

More than 700 patients crowd hospitals in the northwest of the country

; 

War in Ethiopia intensifies

; and so on.

I have been thinking nonstop, day and night, for weeks now. Among the many angry yet simple realizations that seem to come only at night is the thought that, in the years since the signing of the Pretoria Agreement, we had perhaps allowed ourselves to close our eyes, mistaking the absence of full-scale war for peace. Yet beneath the surface, so much was still boiling: disputes over territories that remained contested, disagreements over disarmament, mistrust, and ethnic divisions — the very ones that had made their way even into the streets of Addis. Only this time — 

oh, this time

 — if I squeeze my eyes shut and cover them with my hands, none of this will disappear. What is happening in the country forces me to keep my eyes open, as something that once seemed so far away makes its way into the capital, now more forcefully: evening checkpoints for residents, rumors traveling faster and faster, or 

explosions

 — still unconfirmed — heard near the military headquarters.

And so news reports and newspapers — myself among them, now — proclaim a war at the gates. But whose gates? Those of an Addis, where perhaps it had already been knocking: in the clothes we were told to be ashamed of wearing, in the roads that kept us from our homes, in the mouths of those trying, and trying again, to reach their loved ones in the North.

These days I keep wondering how much of what we are living through is really “sudden.” The dark is something we can make and unmake, my father used to say. He was right. We, myself included, have made the dark for ourselves: While conflict staggered between Tigray, Amhara, and the 

contested territories

, displacing millions of people; while recent attempts at mediation collided with mistrust and accusations of 

partiality

; while signed agreements seemed to give us just enough hope to look away.

Only this time, as the explosions grow louder, we are forced here, in Addis, in Ethiopia, to try to keep our eyes open while elsewhere the world can keep sleeping.

author: Ahmed Ismat Ahmed
title: How a child inherits care
content:
We are sitting at Gallal. It’s in Madinaty, on the edge of Cairo where the buildings are all new and the streets are too wide. The tea is too sweet the way Sudanese tea is supposed to be too sweet when someone else makes it for you. Mahmoud is across from me.

I don’t remember either of us standing up. Only the hug itself, which went on long enough that an Egyptian girl at the next table put down her phone and started crying. She didn’t know us. She cried because whatever passed between two men holding on to each other in the middle of that cafe was apparently visible even to a stranger who had no context at all.

Mahmoud went red immediately — a Sudanese man has no idea what to do with a stranger’s tears — so he pulled out his phone, opened Facebook, and muttered that she was probably crying over some relationship, while the screen in his hand played footage of Khartoum burning. We’re good at that silence now. The silence of being physically tethered to one place while completely living inside another. I kept thinking: Does everyone I love do the same? Carry so much that they stop feeling it, until a stranger has to cry for them?

author: Saif Eddine Ghobr
title: Why does Tunisia become African only when Europe needs it to be?
content:
Tunisia is an African country that has spent much of its modern political imagination looking north. That sounds like a question of identity. In reality, it is a question of power — and more precisely, a practice of domination through classification.

For decades, Tunisia has imagined its economic future through the Mediterranean: European markets, French education, tourism, and European investment. Africa has often appeared somewhere beyond the Sahara, associated with instability, migration, and security.

Europe, however, possesses its own geography of Tunisia — one that shifts depending on what Europe needs from it. When Brussels discusses trade, investment, and political cooperation, Tunisia is a Mediterranean neighbor. When Europe discusses migration, border control, Libya, or the Sahel, Tunisia becomes something else: an African frontier state.

This is not a mere contradiction. This is a deliberate mechanism of geopolitical subordination through classification. Europe does not need Tunisia to be culturally European; it needs Tunisia to be strategically African when African space becomes relevant to European security.

The economic relationship makes this asymmetry impossible to ignore, revealing a genuine policy cage. The European Commission identifies the EU as Tunisia’s largest trading partner. In 2025, the EU accounted for 59.5% of Tunisia’s total trade. Some 73.2% of Tunisian exports went to the EU, while 49.6% of imports came from the European market. The EU is also Tunisia’s largest foreign investor, holding 85% of the country’s foreign direct investment stock.

These figures do not merely describe a successful trading relationship; they reveal an extraordinary concentration of Tunisia’s external economic relations in Europe. When three-quarters of a country’s exports depend on one economic space, that relationship ceases to be mere commerce and becomes an instrument of control, shaping industrial priorities, investment decisions, and the political imagination of what is economically possible.

Europe consequently becomes not simply Tunisia’s largest market, but its economic horizon — where economic dependence transforms into geographical dependence. Africa becomes secondary, not because it is irrelevant, but because Tunisia has spent decades learning to imagine prosperity through a northern market. As Kwame Nkrumah warned in 1965, the most insidious form of domination is control through financial and structural instruments, not direct conquest.

The contradiction becomes sharper when migration enters the picture, exposing the biopolitics of European border management. The EU’s relationship with Tunisia increasingly includes border management, migration control, and the fight against migrant smuggling. European support has included equipment, training, and operational assistance to Tunisian security and coast guard structures.

From Brussels’ perspective, this is cooperation. From a geopolitical standpoint, it is the externalization of Europe’s borders. Europe is not merely helping Tunisia secure its own territory; it is moving part of Europe’s migration-control architecture southward, closer to the routes through which migrants attempt to reach European territory. This is the essence of extraterritorial sovereignty as described by Giorgio Agamben in 2005: the European state exercises its power over human bodies beyond its borders.

This changes the meaning of Tunisia’s geography. Tunisia is no longer simply a neighbor across the Mediterranean; it becomes part of a European security perimeter without becoming part of Europe itself. Tunisia consequently occupies a peculiar geopolitical position: its economic relationship with Europe is framed as partnership, while its position on migration is treated as strategic infrastructure. The Mediterranean neighbor becomes the African frontier.

Yet another geography is beginning to emerge — one that challenges the idea of Tunisia as merely Europe’s southern security buffer. In June 2026, AfCFTA Secretary-General Wamkele Mene visited Tunisia. The visit concluded with an agreed action plan aimed at deepening Tunisia’s trade across Africa.

This matters because it offers Tunisia a role fundamentally different from that assigned to it by the European migration agenda. The African Continental Free Trade Area offers Tunisia the possibility of becoming an economic actor within Africa, rather than a buffer between Europe and Africa. The African Development Bank is pursuing a similar regional logic. In June 2026, the Bank held consultations in Tunis for a new North Africa Regional Integration Strategy designed to deepen economic integration within North Africa and between North Africa and the wider African continent.

This is a radically different understanding of Africa. Africa is not merely the place from which Tunisia receives migrants, security risks, or instability. It is a market. It is a network of cities. It is a space for investment, industrial partnerships, logistics, technology, and political influence. The question is whether Tunisia will treat this geography as a strategy, or merely as an alternative whenever its relationship with Europe becomes difficult. There is a danger in treating Africa as a Plan B, because if Tunisian policymakers look south only when European markets become restrictive, African integration will remain a reaction rather than a strategy.

The choice is not Europe or Africa. Tunisia does not need to abandon its European relationship; its economic links with Europe are too deep, and its geography makes the Mediterranean an unavoidable part of its foreign policy. But Europe cannot be Tunisia’s only horizon.

The real choice is between being an object in someone else’s geography and becoming an actor in one’s own. If Tunisia is African only when Europe needs a border guard, its Africanness has been reduced to a function. If Tunisia discovers Africa only when it needs new markets, Africa becomes a fallback rather than a strategy.

Europe does not merely change Tunisia’s label; it confiscates Tunisia’s agency. By defining Tunisia as Mediterranean when it needs a market and African when it needs a buffer, Europe ensures that Tunisian sovereignty remains conditional — subject to the external power’s geopolitical needs. This is not partnership; it is strategic subordination. Africa is too often presented in European policy as a space from which problems arrive: migrants, instability, terrorism, trafficking, and energy insecurity. But Africa is also a political and economic project being built. The AfCFTA is an attempt to create a continental market; regional integration initiatives are attempting to connect North Africa more effectively with the rest of the continent.

Tunisia is already inside this geography. The question is whether it will remain inside it mainly as a recipient of European security policy, or whether it will begin to act as an African state pursuing its own economic and geopolitical interests. The problem, therefore, is not that Tunisia has forgotten that it is African. The problem is that Tunisia has not yet decided what being African is for — and has allowed external powers to determine when each geography is politically useful.

author: Tosin Durodola
title: Deported to Liberia, again
content:
In 1816, a group of white people in the US created the 

American Society for Colonizing the Free People of Color of the United States

 (later simply the American Colonization Society), aimed at resolving the “problem” of a growing population of free black people in the country. Both slave owners, fearing that large numbers of free black people would lead to slave uprisings, and some white abolitionists, who viewed their presence as either a security threat or a barrier to emancipation, joined hands in a plan to quite literally deport free black Americans and freed slaves to a settlement they hoped to create in the African motherland. 

This is the origin story of the African state of Liberia, one where race, racism, and anti-black slavery meet yet another type of forced movement: deportation. And in a continuum with centuries past, the African continent, which had solved a problem of lack of (free) labor for white US elites and landowners, now solved yet another perceived problem for their descendants: a population of free black people they considered undesirable. As Jonathan Ort 

has shown

, today’s deportation system revives that colonial blueprint.

A little more than 200 years later, an overwhelmingly white US executive power again uses Liberian territory as a deposit for its undesirables, with one difference: the constructed enemy deported from the white nation is anot

author: Babatunde Opeyemi Salami
title: What Nollywood owes the ancestors
content:
In June 2025, in Lagos, I sat down with custodians of Yoruba masquerading traditions, and I asked each of them a version of the same question: “What do you think about masquerades appearing in Nigerian films?” Each time, the answer was a flat no.

I grew up in Lagos and have spent years studying Yoruba masquerading traditions, particularly 

Eyo

 and 

Igunnuko

. With support from the Ebrahim Hussein Fellowship and the Aliko Songolo Award, I conducted formal interviews at the Bajulaye and Alagbeji palaces and at the Igunnuko shrines in Epetedo and Alaguntan to understand where this resistance comes from. More importantly, I sought to know what it means for Nollywood to keep returning to these figures despite the pushback.

Foundational cultural theorists of the 1930s and 1940s grappled with a similar question of what happens when a sacred or ritual object is copied, restaged, or transferred into a new medium. In 1944, Theodor Adorno and Max Horkheimer believed that mechanical reproduction drains ritual objects of their meaning, while Walter Benjamin had argued the opposite about a decade earlier. For Benjamin, reproduction could free art from ritual’s grip rather than hollow it out. The reality of this tension is a concept that my fieldwork explores.

To understand the resistance to masquerade remediation in film, you first have to understand what a masquerade is to its custo

author: AbdouMaliq Simone
title: The radical openness of the popular economy
content:
Urban Africa is constantly finding ways to thicken urban life with new resourcefulness: from makeshift maker labs to the vast associations of traders with their own home-grown, expansive financial systems — where remittances circulate alongside locally generated credit and savings — to self-generated webs of electricity and water provisioning under the radar, to neighborhood investments in shared containers of imported goods, to local circuits of production and distribution of foodstuffs, intermingled with diverse labor arrangements across regions and borders. These are what we call popular economies.

Residents inhabit environments replete with different land statuses, regulatory frameworks, histories of economic specialization, repositories of cultural memory, behavioral styles, and social arrangements. Urban popular economies entail how these various components of an archive are pieced together and interrelated to produce specific mobilities and access to resources and opportunities. It is a move toward an expanded diversification of how accumulation, social reproduction, and livelihood get built. African cities are renowned for their informal sectors, self-built neighborhoods, as well as histories of piracy, brigandage, circumvention, smuggling, and subversion. The popular economy intersects with these elements in a continuous unfolding and elaboration of more overarching e

author: Yasmine Benabderrahmane
title: Is "khawa khawa" a North African myth?
content:
In the haze of 

el ghorba

 — the strangeness and alienation of living abroad — I gravitate toward the Maghrebi diaspora. For a moment, we relax our tongues from the unnatural twists of Arabic dialects foreign to us and speak in the Maghrebi 

darija

s. Desperate to latch onto whatever whispers of home exist elsewhere, we claim that we are 

khawa khawa

.

Among the Algerians, Moroccans, and Tunisians, 

khawa khawa

 is an official nod to an unofficial alliance, loosely translating to 

brotherhood

. It is an ode to our shared cultures and history in the face of North African identity discourses.

But what began as a salve for colonialism was lost in the monotonous chants for brotherhood.

Before the 19th century, North African states were “undefined” to European cartographers and authorities alike. Hence, like the concept of the Middle East and the Sahel, the Maghreb was prone to imperial invention. Unsurprisingly, this coincided with the Scramble for Africa — when the insatiable greed of European colonial powers took interest in dividing the African continent among themselves.

Encompassing other colonial legacies, the borders born out of the Scramble engineered the ethnic rivalries that persist in Africa today. Through the newly devised borders and the infamous “divide and conquer” regimes, the Maghreb was branded as distinct.

Despite the existing racial diversity of the region, the French colonial regimes rebranded the Maghreb as a biracial society: Amazigh or Arab. While the Amazigh identity was mislabeled in proximity to the whiteness of Europe, the Arab identity became an accusation of settler colonialism. North Africa became a geographic body for the Francophonie world, distanced from its neighboring regions’ cultures, politics, and society.

In 1962, Algeria — the last of France’s Maghrebi colonies — declared independence. In the years that followed, the Maghrebi people looked inwards and toward rebuilding the identity of North Africa. Thus, 

khawa khawa

 was born and reinforced by the diaspora that fled their homes in the wake of political instability. It became a card dealt in moments of desperation to bond to something, or someone, that vaguely resembled home.

Khawa khawa

, and the brotherhood that blossomed with it, became the means to redress an identity obscured by European colonialism.

True 

khawa khawa

 culture demands communal harmony void of ego. But when politics becomes inevitably entangled in the national identity of communities, the culture of Maghrebi brotherhood falls flat.

Shortly after 1962, newly independent Algeria and Morocco fell into border disputes. The following decades spiraled into attempted land grabs, fits of cultural monopolies, and accusations of expansionist ambitions. In response, the people cried out 

khawa khawa; our governments do not define our brotherhood

!

But too often, the politics override the social bonds of Algerians and Moroccans (and occasionally, Tunisians). With the rise of the internet, discourse shifted, and social media became a useful mirror for the abstractions of the Maghrebi identity.

Most recently, the 

khawa khawa

 culture was dramatically pronounced dead on social media platforms, following the 2025 African Cup of Nations (AFCON). Almost overnight, the football tournament became a litmus test for Algerian-Moroccan relations and spiraled into a warped perception of North African relations. A futile online back-and-forth that began as shared banter turned into personal attacks and political scrutiny.

The post-AFCON 

guerre

 between Algerians and Moroccans — which coincided with the recent 

UN support

 for Moroccan plans over the Western Sahara, disapproved by the Algerian government — is a recurring phenomenon of how Maghrebi culture wages war parallel to the political tensions of its respective countries. Despite the adamant denial, online Maghrebi communities fall into the habit of using our governments to verify the authenticity of 

khawa khawa

.

The problem rests in the fact that both communities — Algerian and Moroccan — fall into the habit of claiming the minority of hateful comments as the consensus among the entirety of both nations. We see assertions made that we cannot prove, except that they are too insulting and their wounds far too inflicting to recover from. It has become a pattern of malice between both nations that resurfaces regardless of how loudly 

khawa khawa

 is chanted.

Perhaps the fault is also in the fragility of how we materialize our cultural bonds. We claim that 

khawa khawa

 is an Islamic brotherhood, yet some grow secular. In the absence of religious backing, 

khawa khawa

 becomes a proverb of the old world. Then, we claim that 

khawa khawa

 is a call for pan-Arabism, yet some grow weary of Arabization. In the face of the Amazigh renaissance, 

khawa khawa

 becomes a proverb of the imperial world.

Perhaps, much like the colonists, we, too, have confined the Maghrebi identity to arbitrary borders of existence, repackaged in the 

khawa khawa

 culture, while we feed into the delusions of European-drawn borders. And so, 

khawa khawa

 becomes a hollow reminder of colonial fractures.

While we cannot divorce our identities from politics, the Maghrebi community must forgo the egos that are founded in political symbolism. We should understand that an enforceable unity can exist if we acknowledge that each community upholds legitimate, separate interests.

As long as we treat 

khawa khawa

 as nothing more than a symbolic slogan that dissipates under the legacy of French colonialism and the futility of online disputes, Maghrebi relations will live on as a North African myth of brotherhood.

Khawa khawa

 is a brotherhood that encompasses the lived and nuanced identities of the Maghreb; let us not reduce it to mere grounds of conflict for North African communities.

Alas, in 

el ghorba

, it is always among the Maghrebi diaspora that I find remnants of my home.

author: Anooradha Iyer Siddiqi
title: Reading List: Anooradha Iyer Siddiqi
content:
We are taught to think of a refugee camp as an object produced in an instant, only in response to an emergency — one brought on, perhaps, by those seeking refuge. We are taught that refugee environments are provisional and abject, moreover, to be naturalized as such within the African landscape — 

as

 the African landscape. We are taught to misread migrant spaces as lacking history or architectural expression. To counter these misdirections, 

Architecture of Migration: The Dadaab Refugee Camps and Humanitarian Settlement

 looks closely at the complex settlements, ecologies, domesticities, archives, and material aesthetics. In Ifo, Dagahaley, and Hagadera camps, established in 1991 by the Kenyan government and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees at Dadaab, Kenya, in lands shared with Somalia and Ethiopia, the book finds African, Muslim, and Afro-Asian aesthetic worlds and a historical repository of partition, sedentarization, and migration. Dadaab forms a material afterlife of events long unfolding, through colonial and postcolonial time and space, and in multiple registers, aesthetic as well as social.

My book is grounded in 14 years of feminist and critical collective practice and research (see 

Cohabitations

, 

Dadaab Commons

, 

Feminist Architectural Histories of Migration

, 

Insurgent Domesticities

, and 

Settlement

). While researching in dozen

author: Eliel Peterson
title: Death as liberation
content:
Death as liberation is hardly a comfortable political proposition to digest. In a world where Black death is often the common condition, there is a well-established insistence on our living. So what do we make of two of Africa’s greatest filmmakers, Ousmane Sembène and Souleymane Cissé, whose earliest cinematic visions, expressed through their respective debut features 

Black Girl

 (1966) and 

Den Muso

 (1975), center on the suffering, alienation, and eventual deaths of Black women?

Sembène’s 

Black Girl

 is preoccupied with racial violence and the economic exploitation that continues to structure relations between Senegal and France. The film follows Diouana, a young Senegalese woman who accepts employment with a white French family and travels to Antibes believing she is embarking on a new life. While Cissé’s 

Den Muso

, turns inward, examining interpersonal violence and the ways patriarchal power consumes family life and communities, weakening the broader social fabric of a nation. The film follows Tenin, a mute young woman who becomes pregnant after being raped, exposing the brutal underbelly of the patriarchal violence imposed upon her. Despite the differences in their circumstances, both films position death as a troubling possibility of liberation for their central characters.

Tenin (Dounamba Dany Coulibaly) in a still from Souleymane Cissé’s 

Den Muso

 (1975

author: Afolabi Adekaiyaoja
title: Forward, but for whom?
content:
I have spent this week reflecting on African football. Qualifiers for the next Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) have begun, the identity of the reigning champions still awaits a ruling from the Court of Arbitration for Sport, and Nigeria begins its campaign without a federation board, after its president and executive committee 

resigned in August

 — a rare case of Nigerian football administrators paying a price for failure, though, as I will argue, not quite the accountability it first appears. None of it can be separated from the politics and money that will shape next year’s FIFA presidential election.

Weeks after the 2026 World Cup in North America, FIFA unveiled a plan to sell a stake in the tournament’s commercial rights to private investors. The proposal would have seen a new entity, FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), take over FIFA’s broadcast, sponsorship, ticketing, and licensing operations. FIFA would keep control and sell minority stakes to outside investors, raising up to $4.2 billion against a $20 billion valuation. The lead investor was reportedly 

Thrive

, a firm founded by Joshua Kushner, whose brother Jared is US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law. To win the member associations’ approval, FIFA promised to raise each one’s development allocation for 2027–2030 from about $8 million to $20 million, with an optional further $20 million paid up front. author: B Camminga
title: We are not a novelty
content:
Trans and gender-diverse people are routinely told that what they are is new — a sudden emergence, a recent contagion. In South Africa, this claim circulates with increasing force: In the 

surge of Christian fundamentalist organizing against trans rights

, in the transphobic slurs directed at a trans contestant on 

Big Brother Mzansi

 earlier this year, and in the pronouncements of 

prominent political figures

 who have characterized transgender rights as a form of 

“woke” ideology

. The implication is always the same: that we are a novelty. And novelties do not deserve the weight of rights.

The historical record tells a different story.

In 1815, a young British military surgeon arrived at the Cape Colony. 

James Barry

 was cantankerous, flamboyant, and conspicuously short. During his time at the Cape, he performed what is believed to be the first cesarean section in southern Africa in which both mother and child survived. The child was named after him: James Barry Munnik, who would grow up to become the grandfather of J. B. M. Hertzog — founder of the National Party in 1914 and one of the principal architects of apartheid.

J. B. M. was also the namesake of the hertzoggie, the apricot-jam-filled tartlet. When he reneged on promises, the Cape Malay community responded with the 

twee gevreetjie

: a coconut-topped protest cookie whose name means, in Afrikaans, “two-

author: Marta Mboka Tveit
title: Utopia is not a metaphor
content:
The recent popularity of the term “Afrotopia” inspired me to revisit Thomas More’s original 

Utopia

 (1516). Rereading the novel led me to rethink what we mean when we talk about ideology, future-casting, and visioning as praxis.

“Utopia” or “utopic” is today a widely used term across a variety of fields and contexts. People often use the term derogatorily, as a tired metaphor, carrying connotations of naiveté or veiled dystopian impulses. It gestures vaguely toward paradise, toward the promised land, but carries with it a whiff of the opposite. Don’t be naive, the contemporary connotation seems to say; don’t fall for the lies, don’t dream too big. Recently, daring scholarship has given the term a new, promised-land spin: for instance, in Felwine Sarr’s bold essay 

Afrotopia

 (2020), a poetic call for an African utopian philosophy of self-reinvention for the 21st century, and, more recently, in Joseph Agbakoba and Marita Rainsborough’s 

Beyond Decolonial African Philosophy

 (2025).

But reading 

Utopia

, I was surprised by how concrete and policy-oriented the novel is. Its protagonist, Raphael Hythloday (sort of an early anthropologist), is in a debate with a fictionalized version of More himself and some others, and ends up talking about his visit to an island called Utopia, a visit that has profoundly changed him. Hythloday talks about how they organize life there, a

author: William Shoki
title: Brazil’s racket society
content:
Brazil’s presidential election is headed for a runoff. In the first round on October 4, far-right Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, edged out President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva 47 percent to 45 percent. The right also consolidated its hold on Congress, with Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party now the largest bloc in the Senate. The result came despite Flávio’s thin record, his documented ties to Rio de Janeiro’s militias, and his father’s 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election.

As Latin America’s largest economy and its most populous democracy, Brazil has long served as a bellwether for the region, and increasingly for the world. Analysts of neoliberalism have used “Brazilianization” to describe a future of informal work, fortified elites, and hollowed-out states that they see arriving in the global North. The outcome of the runoff will help decide whether Brazil holds out against a regional turn toward Trump-aligned strongmen, a wave that has already swept Argentina, Ecuador, and, most recently, Colombia.

The stakes are high. Lula’s third term delivered growth, rising wages, and record-low unemployment, but it was hemmed in by a hostile Congress, and household debt and the cost of living kept climbing. Meanwhile, the Trump administration has intervened with unusual openness. It has imposed punitive tariffs and sa

author: Folashade Roberts
title: Old Nollywood 2.0
content:
Scroll to the comments under the movie 

Love in Every Word

 on YouTube, and you will find viewers from Lagos to London, Accra, Houston, and beyond, tagging sisters to “come and watch this.” Even though the movie had no cinema release and no streaming deal, it reached 15 million views within a week of its March 2025 release on the Omoni Oboli TV YouTube channel. It reached roughly 30 million by year’s end. Actress and filmmaker Omoni Oboli and her business partner, Tomi Adeoye, launched Omoni Oboli TV in December 2023. Since then, the channel has gained more than two million subscribers. The success of 

Love in Every Word

 and its sequel pushed their YouTube television channel past 182 million total views across 550 videos, and it was named YouTube Nigeria’s Top Creator Channel of 2025.

The story and style of 

Love in Every Word

 are typical of Nollywood cinema, but there is something about the success of its format that raises questions. Is it an example of a new paradigm for how we understand the present-day movie industry in Nigeria? Or is it marking a return to the spirit of the original Nollywood? Does this format’s mix of “New Nollywood” and “Old Nollywood” betoken a new concept? Perhaps we could call it “Old Nollywood 2.0.”

author: Joshua W.J. Brown
title: What replaced the slave trade?
content:
The first thought came out ugly because the event itself was ugly: tens of thousands of people moving at once toward Ceuta, a Spanish city in North Africa, beaches and roads filling, people dying, police lines folding, rumors moving faster than governments. I looked at Morocco on one side, Spain and the European Union on the other, and thought: What exactly is being traded here?

I don’t mean that migrants are slaves. They aren’t. That isn’t the argument, and collapsing the two would make the argument stupid. Slavery means ownership: a human being captured, bought, sold, inherited, coerced, and legally treated as property. A migrant is not somebody else’s property simply because a state wants to stop him, move her, return them, admit them, or keep them out.

What I’m asking is what came after. What happens to economies and states that once participated in systems where human movement itself generated external value? Does abolition erase that logic, or does value move somewhere else?

Ceuta is where the question became impossible for me to ignore. 

On July 30, more than 70,000 people crossed or attempted to cross

 from Morocco into the Spanish enclave in the largest such surge the border has seen. 

Current reporting doesn’t support the easy conspiracy version

. Economic frustration mattered. False claims spread online that the border was open. Smugglers and informal networks

author: Kévin Drif
title: The North African family French critics couldn’t see
content:
Since her 2016 debut feature 

Raw

, the French auteur Julia Ducournau’s films have been a staple of the body horror genre. Her movies reflect an unapologetic approach to exploring physical transformation and the “monstrous feminine,” an idea coined by feminist film scholar Barbara Creed to underscore the significance of gender and sexuality in the construction of monstrosity. In Ducournau’s films, female characters strive for emancipation from social and familial norms through cannibalism or transhumanism. Yet while 

Raw

 and her sophomore feature 

Titane

 (2021) center white protagonists, 

Alpha

 (2025), her third film, foregrounds the complex dynamic of a family of North African descent, marking a significant departure for the auteur. Curiously, this demographic difference has been almost entirely absent from discussions of the film.

Set between the 1980s and 1990s, 

Alpha

 follows its 13-year-old eponymous character; her mother, who is a doctor; and her uncle Amin as they confront a mysterious virus that transforms bodies into blue-veined marmoreal statues that eventually turn to dust. Critics have understandably focused on the epidemic narrative, the stigma attached to the infected, and its evocation of the AIDS crisis, but in doing so, they have overlooked another dimension of the story: 

Alpha

 is one of the few contemporary French films to place a family of

author: Feven Merid
title: Where the mouse eats the cat
content:
“Welcome to the Central Prison of Douala,” La PJ, an inmate and a star of the documentary 

Jail Time Records

, says in an opening scene of the film. “The place where the mouse eats the cat.” Dione Roach, one of the film’s directors, offered me an interpretation: “The world is upside down in prison; the mouse can be more shrewd,” she said. The intimate glimpse into the Central Prison of Douala, also known as New Bell Prison, does indeed reveal an upside-down world. Like many prisons, its inmates recreate the contours of outside life on the inside, but in New Bell it’s taken to another level. There are actual neighborhoods like the Latin Quarter, home to the Emperor and his gang known as the Latinos, and the Base, where the prisoners who make up the quasi police squad reside. There’s a marketplace for people to sell fried foods and taxis, except these taxis are inmates who swiftly run through the congested prison to hand-deliver messages. They even have a “homeless” population, those who must sleep outside in the courtyard because there aren’t enough beds. Their neighborhood is dubbed House of the Penguins.

This all comes into focus when you learn New Bell is notoriously overcrowded — it was built for 800 people but currently holds almost 6,000. Thus, the prison has been transformed into a mini city, colloquially referred to by inmates as the 11th province of Cameroon (there a

author: Husam Mahjoub
title: The war Abu Dhabi didn’t need to fight
content:
Several outside actors have stoked the flames of war in Sudan, but none has had as great an impact as the United Arab Emirates. The evidence of its destructive role is overwhelming, but the Gulf kingdom’s Western allies have turned a blind eye to it.

At one time or another, Sudanese governments have hosted, armed, or tolerated rebels and opposition groups from all of the country’s neighbors, from Egypt and Libya to Uganda and Ethiopia. Sudan’s neighbors have repaid the favor, and a range of outside actors are now involved in the Sudanese civil war.

Key supporters of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) include Chad, Ethiopia, Uganda, Kenya, and South Sudan. Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and Eritrea support the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the de facto government. Among all the external actors, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) is the most consequential, even though it has the least reason to be involved.

Every other external actor has a stake in Sudan that derives from geography, security exposure, or the influx of Sudanese refugees. Even Saudi Arabia, while not a land neighbor, shares the Red Sea coastline with Sudan and has a direct interest in stabilizing its western maritime frontier.

The UAE has no security interest, no shared border or river, and no reason to be concerned about refugees reaching Emirati territory. We can only understand its role in Sudan as part of a broader subimpe
